claim: Enantiornithines were the dominant birds of the Mesozoic.
source: Enantiornithines were the dominant birds of the Mesozoic, but understanding of their diet is still tenuous.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the abstract without specific supporting data in the manuscript.

claim: Understanding of enantiornithine diet is still tenuous.
source: Enantiornithines were the dominant birds of the Mesozoic, but understanding of their diet is still tenuous.
evidence: This is supported by the limited number of species examined (12 of over 100) as stated in the introduction.

claim: Bohaiornithidae are famous for their large size and powerfully built teeth and claws.
source: We introduce new data on the enantiornithine family Bohaiornithidae, famous for their large size and powerfully built teeth and claws.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature and morphological descriptions in the manuscript.

claim: Bohaiornis and Parabohaiornis are similar to living plant-eating birds.
source: We find bohaiornithids to be more ecologically diverse than any other enantiornithine family: Bohaiornis and Parabohaiornis are similar to living plant-eating birds
evidence: This is supported by body mass, mechanical advantage, FEA, and skull morphometric analyses presented in the Results and Discussion sections.

claim: Longusunguis resembles raptorial carnivores.
source: Longusunguis resembles raptorial carnivores
evidence: This is supported by pedal traditional morphometric analysis showing affinity with large raptors and recurved teeth morphology.

claim: Zhouornis is similar to both fruit-eating birds and generalist feeders.
source: Zhouornis is similar to both fruit-eating birds and generalist feeders
evidence: This is supported by FEA showing strong jaws, MA analysis, and body mass data presented in the Results section.

claim: Shenqiornis and Sulcavis plausibly ate fish, plants, or a mix of both.
source: Shenqiornis and Sulcavis plausibly ate fish, plants, or a mix of both
evidence: This is supported by MA and FEA analyses showing affinities with multiple diet groups as discussed in the Results section.

claim: The ancestral enantiornithine bird was predicted to have been a generalist which ate a wide variety of foods.
source: We predict the ancestral enantiornithine bird to have been a generalist which ate a wide variety of foods.
evidence: This is based on ancestral state reconstruction of body mass, MA, FEA, and pedal TM data as presented in Table 7 and Table 8.

claim: By the Early Cretaceous, enantiornithine birds had diversified into a variety of ecological niches like crown birds after the K-Pg extinction.
source: By the Early Cretaceous, enantiornithine birds had diversified into a variety of ecological niches like crown birds after the K-Pg extinction
evidence: This is supported by the diversity of diets identified across enantiornithine families and comparison to crown bird diversification timelines.

claim: Traits unique to crown birds cannot completely explain their ecological success.
source: adding to the evidence that traits unique to crown birds cannot completely explain their ecological success
evidence: This is inferred from the finding that enantiornithines achieved similar ecological diversity without crown bird traits like edentulism or cranial kinesis.

claim: Dietary evolution within crown birds is a complex mosaic.
source: The diet of crown birds is extremely broad, and dietary evolution within the crown is a complex mosaic (Felice et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Felice et al., 2019.

claim: Dietary evolution in birds outside the crown is poorly understood.
source: However, dietary evolution in birds outside the crown is poorly understood, largely because the diet of most Mesozoic birds remains speculative
evidence: This is supported by citation to Miller and Pittman, 2021 and the limited number of studies on Mesozoic bird diet.

claim: Only 12 of the over 100 described enantiornithine species have been examined for diet.
source: This progress only amounts to an examination of 12 of the over 100 described enantiornithine species (Pittman, 2020a), though.
evidence: This is stated as a fact with citation to Pittman, 2020a.

claim: Enantiornithines were the most abundant and speciose birds in the Cretaceous.
source: The most progress has been made among enantiornithines (Miller et al., 2022; Miller et al., 2023; Clark et al., 2023), the most abundant and speciose birds in the Cretaceous (Pittman, 2020a).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Pittman, 2020a.

claim: Bohaiornithids have iridescent colouration.
source: Bohaiornithids are iconic among enantiornithines for their robust teeth, large claws, large size (Wang, 2014a), and iridescent colouration (Peteya et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Peteya et al., 2017.

claim: Bohaiornithid robust teeth have led to interpretations of the clade as durophagous.
source: Their robust teeth have led the clade to be interpreted as durophagous (O'Connor and Chiappe, 2011a; O'Connor et al., 2013; Chiappe and Meng, 2016; Zhou et al., 2021)
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous literature.

claim: Bohaiornithid large claws and large body size have led to raptorial interpretations.
source: while their large claws and large body size lead to raptorial interpretations (Wang, 2014a; Chiappe and Meng, 2016; Li et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Bohaiornithidae is the most speciose family of enantiornithine birds.
source: With the recently described Beiguornis (Wang, 2022a), Bohaiornithidae is the most speciose family of enantiornithine birds.
evidence: This is stated as a fact with citation to Wang, 2022a.

claim: Size has a strong effect on birds' diets.
source: Size has a strong effect on birds' diets (Navalón et al., 2019; Pigot et al., 2020; Natale and Slater, 2022)
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: Mechanical advantage of the jaw looks at trade-offs between bite speed and force.
source: Most commonly, the functional index used in ecology is MA of the jaw, looking at trade-offs between bite speed and force (Stayton, 2006; Corbin et al., 2015; Adams et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: If an FEA model experiences less strain under the same relative load as another model, its shape can withstand a greater force before failure.
source: If a model experiences less strain under the same relative load as another model, its shape can withstand a greater force before failure.
evidence: This is a fundamental principle of finite element analysis supported by engineering knowledge.

claim: Traditional morphometrics of claw curvature and relative size can differentiate between non-raptorial and raptorial birds.
source: Here, measurements are taken of the curvature and relative size of pedal unguals which can differentiate between non-raptorial and raptorial birds (Csermely and Rossi, 2006; Fowler et al., 2009; Csermely et al., 2012; Cobb and Sellers, 2020)
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: The comparative dataset includes nearly 200 extant birds.
source: These proxies are of little use without reference values, so comparative data is taken from nearly 200 extant birds (Miller et al., 2022; Miller et al., 2023)
evidence: This is stated as a fact describing the study's methodology.

claim: The extant bird dataset was expanded to 8758 of the 9994 recognised species of birds using the AVONET database.
source: With the recent publication of the bird database AVONET (Tobias et al., 2022), we are able to expand our dataset comparing mass and diet to 8758 of the 9994 recognised species of birds.
evidence: This is stated as a fact describing the study's methodology with citation to the data source.

claim: Bird masses separated into four significantly different combinations of diet categories.
source: Bird masses separated into four significantly different combinations of diet categories using phylogenetic honest significant differences (HSD)
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of the AVONET dataset as described in the Methods and Results sections.

claim: The cut-off point between nectarivores and granivores/invertivores is 9 g (95% CI 8–10 g).
source: between a and b, 9 g (95% confidence interval [CI] 8–10 g)
evidence: This is derived from statistical analysis of body mass data as shown in Figure 3.

claim: The cut-off point between granivores/invertivores and frugivores/generalists is 56 g (95% CI 41–63 g).
source: between b and c, 56 g (95% CI 41–63 g)
evidence: This is derived from statistical analysis of body mass data as shown in Figure 3.

claim: The cut-off point between frugivores/generalists and folivores/tetrapod hunters is 265 g (95% CI 162–303 g).
source: between c and d, 265 g (95% CI 162–303 g)
evidence: This is derived from statistical analysis of body mass data as shown in Figure 3.

claim: Bohaiornithid body masses range from 91 g to 905 g, with a mean of 287 g.
source: Estimated bohaiornithid body masses are provided in Table 3. Masses range from 91 g to 905 g, x̄ = 287 g
evidence: This is based on body mass estimation methods applied to bohaiornithid specimens as detailed in Table 3.

claim: Excluding the largest Zhouornis specimen, bohaiornithid masses range from 91 to 406 g, with a mean of 248 g.
source: With the larger Zhouornis excluded, masses range from 91 to 406 g, x̄ = 248 g.
evidence: This is based on body mass estimation methods applied to bohaiornithid specimens as detailed in Table 3.

claim: Significant phylogenetic signal was found in extant bird mass, with trends resembling those expected under a Brownian motion model of evolution (K = 0.93).
source: Significant phylogenetic signal was found in extant bird mass, with trends resembling those expected under a Brownian motion model of evolution (K = 0.93; Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is based on phylogenetic comparative analysis of the body mass data.

claim: Bohaiornithids generally have low anterior jaw-closing mechanical advantage (AMA), posterior jaw-closing mechanical advantage (PMA), relative articular offset (AO), and relative maximum mandibular height (MMH) relative to living birds.
source: Bohaiornithids generally have low anterior jaw-closing mechanical advantage (AMA), posterior jaw-closing mechanical advantage (PMA), relative articular offset (AO), and relative maximum mandibular height (MMH) relative to living birds
evidence: This is based on mechanical advantage measurements from reconstructed skulls as shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Most bohaiornithids have a low jaw-opening mechanical advantage (OMA), but Bohaiornis has a high OMA.
source: Most bohaiornithids also have a low jaw-opening mechanical advantage (OMA), but Bohaiornis has a high OMA.
evidence: This is based on mechanical advantage measurements from reconstructed skulls as shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Significant phylogenetic signal is present in the extant MA dataset overall.
source: Significant phylogenetic signal is present in the extant MA dataset overall (Supplementary file 1)
evidence: This is based on phylogenetic comparative analysis of the mechanical advantage data.

claim: Bohaiornithid MWAM strain is low (89–156 µε, x̄ = 128 µε).
source: MWAM strain of bohaiornithids is low (89–156 µε, x̄ = 128 µε)
evidence: This is based on finite element analysis of reconstructed skulls as shown in Figure 5.

claim: Bohaiornis and Zhouornis experience less strain under loading than any extant carnivorous bird in this study (min = 105 µε).
source: with Bohaiornis and Zhouornis experiencing less strain under loading that any extant carnivorous bird in this study (min = 105 µε).
evidence: This is based on comparison of FEA results between bohaiornithids and extant birds as shown in Figure 5.

claim: No significant phylogenetic signal was recovered in the extant FEA data.
source: No significant phylogenetic signal was recovered in the extant FEA data (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is based on phylogenetic comparative analysis of the FEA data.

claim: Sulcavis plots among large raptors in pedal TM PCA.
source: In PCA, Sulcavis plots among large raptors
evidence: This is based on principal component analysis of pedal traditional morphometric data as shown in Figure 7.

claim: Both Parabohaiornis individuals plot among non-raptorial perching birds in pedal TM PCA.
source: both Parabohaiornis individuals plot among non-raptorial perching birds
evidence: This is based on principal component analysis of pedal traditional morphometric data as shown in Figure 7.

claim: Significant phylogenetic signal is present in the extant pedal TM dataset overall.
source: Significant phylogenetic signal is present in the extant pedal TM dataset overall (Supplementary file 1)
evidence: This is based on phylogenetic comparative analysis of the pedal TM data.

claim: Granivores and tetrapod hunters tend to have relatively short rostra (rostrum length/skull length <0.8).
source: Granivores and tetrapod hunters tend to have relatively short rostra (rostrum length/skull length <0.8)
evidence: This is based on skull traditional morphometric analysis as shown in Figure 8.

claim: Folivores, nectarivores, and piscivores tend to have more elongate rostra (rostrum length/skull length >0.8).
source: while folivores, nectarivores, and piscivores tend to have more elongate rostra (rostrum length/skull length >0.8).
evidence: This is based on skull traditional morphometric analysis as shown in Figure 8.

claim: Nectarivores have distinctly elongate skulls (relative skull length >4.5), exclusively true for hummingbirds (Trochilidae).
source: Nectarivores have distinctly elongate skulls (relative skull length >4.5), though this is exclusively true for hummingbirds (Trochilidae).
evidence: This is based on skull traditional morphometric analysis as shown in Figure 8.

claim: Bohaiornithids display distinctly short skulls (relative skull length <1.6).
source: Bohaiornithids display distinctly short skulls (relative skull length <1.6)
evidence: This is based on skull traditional morphometric analysis as shown in Figure 8.

claim: Zhouornis displays the shortest skull relative to body mass of any taxon sampled.
source: with Zhouornis displaying the shortest skull relative to body mass of any taxon sampled.
evidence: This is based on skull traditional morphometric analysis as shown in Figure 8.

claim: The common ancestor of Avisauridae is recovered as 100% likely to be a vertivore.
source: The common ancestor of Avisauridae is recovered as 100% likely to be a vertivore.
evidence: This is based on ancestral state reconstruction as shown in Figure 9.

claim: The common ancestor of Bohaiornithidae is recovered as 34% likely to be an herbivore, 33% likely to be a vertivore, and 33% likely to be an omnivore.
source: The common ancestor of Bohaiornithidae is recovered as 34% likely to be an herbivore, 33% likely to be a vertivore, and 33% likely to be an omnivore.
evidence: This is based on ancestral state reconstruction as shown in Figure 9.

claim: The common ancestor of Longipterygidae is recovered as 100% likely to be an invertivore.
source: The common ancestor of Longipterygidae is recovered as 100% likely to be an invertivore.
evidence: This is based on ancestral state reconstruction as shown in Figure 9.

claim: The diet of the common ancestor of Pengornithidae is recovered as 99% unknown.
source: The diet of the common ancestor of Pengornithidae is recovered as 99% unknown, with the next most likely diet invertivory at 0.02%.

claim: The diet of the common ancestor of all Enantiornithes is recovered as 99% unknown.
source: The same is true for the common ancestor of all Enantiornithes.
evidence: This is based on ancestral state reconstruction as shown in Figure 9.

claim: Bohaiornis has jaws highly reminiscent of avian folivores.
source: Bohaiornis has jaws highly reminiscent of avian folivores
evidence: This is based on multiple lines of evidence including MA, FEA, and skull TM as discussed in the Discussion section.

claim: The most uniquely folivorous trait of Bohaiornis is a high OMA.
source: As noted in the MA discussion, the most uniquely folivorous trait of this taxon is a high OMA.
evidence: This is based on mechanical advantage analysis comparing Bohaiornis to extant birds.

claim: The PMA of Bohaiornis is below any extant folivore (0.16 lower jaw PMA and 0.09 upper jaw PMA, vs a folivore minimum of 0.24 lower jaw PMA and 0.18 upper jaw PMA).
source: While the PMA of Bohaiornis is below that of any studied folivore, its jaw strength in FEA is also similar to that of folivores.

claim: The hoatzin (Opisthocomus hoazin) and southern screamer (Chauna torquata) serve as the most likely extant analogues for Bohaiornis.
source: These two taxa serve as the most likely extant analogues for Bohaiornis
evidence: This is based on similarity in OMA, MWAM strain, and flight style as discussed in the text.

claim: Parabohaiornis has strong herbivorous affinities, though they are less clear than those in Bohaiornis.
source: Parabohaiornis has strong herbivorous affinities, though they are less clear than those in Bohaiornis.
evidence: This is based on MA and FEA analyses showing similarity to swallowing granivores and folivores.

claim: Sandgrouse (Pteroclidae) may serve as an extant analogy for Parabohaiornis as swallowing granivores in the 200–300 g mass range.
source: Sandgrouse (Pteroclidae) may serve as an extant analogy as swallowing granivores in the 200–300 g mass range
evidence: This is based on comparison of body mass and jaw morphology between Parabohaiornis and sandgrouse.

claim: Crops and gizzards have previously been inferred to be absent in Enantiornithes.
source: Crops and gizzards have previously been inferred to be absent in Enantiornithes (O'Connor and Zhou, 2020c)

claim: Structures now recognised as plant propagules have been identified in seven enantiornithine specimens.
source: Structures now recognised as plant propagules (Mayr et al., 2020) have been identified in seven enantiornithine specimens (O'Connor et al., 2014).

claim: In figured enantiornithine specimens, plant propagules are preserved either in the lowest thoracic or pelvic region.
source: in these figured specimens the propagules are preserved either in the lowest thoracic (STM 10-45 and STM 11-80) or pelvic (STM 29-8 and STM 10-12) region.

claim: Zhouornis has the strongest jaw among bohaiornithids.
source: Zhouornis has the strongest jaw among bohaiornithids (Figure 5)

claim: Longusunguis has more recurved teeth than other bohaiornithids.
source: Longusunguis notably has more recurved teeth than other bohaiornithids (Figures 4 and 6 in Zhou et al., 2021)

claim: Recurved teeth are associated with carnivory.
source: which is associated with carnivory (Button and Zanno, 2020).

source: Our data suggest that bohaiornithids cover a greater ecological breadth than previously studied enantiornithine families (Figure 9).

claim: Longipterygids are reconstructed as mainly invertivorous with variability in foraging environment.
source: Longipterygids are reconstructed as mainly invertivorous with variability in foraging environment (Miller et al., 2022; Figure 1, left

source: pengornithids are reconstructed as generally piscivorous with Pengornis diversifying into a more generalist and macrocarnivorous diet (Miller et al., 2023; Figure 1, right).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Miller et al., 2023 and depicted in Figure 1.

claim: The increased dietary breadth in Bohaiornithidae appears to stem from increased strength in the bohaiornithid skull.
source: The increased dietary breadth in Bohaiornithidae appears to stem from increased strength in the bohaiornithid skull.

claim: Much ecological change and diversification occurred within Enantiornithes by 120 Ma.

claim: Crown birds may have been slower to occupy the same ecological breadth as their Mesozoic counterparts.

claim: The extant MA and FEA dataset consists of 141 birds across multiple diet categories.
source: No additional extant birds are sampled for MA or FEA beyond the dataset of Miller et al., 2023, meaning these datasets consist of 141 birds: 9 folivores, 17 frugivores, 17 generalists, 8 husking granivores, 8 swallowing granivores, 43 invertivores, 7 nectarivores, 15 piscivores, 8 scavengers, and 9 tetrapod hunters.
evidence: This is stated as a fact describing the study's dataset.

claim: The extant pedal TM dataset includes 66 birds across multiple ecological categories.
source: In total, the extant TM dataset includes 66 birds: 9 ground birds, 23 non-raptorial perching birds, 4 shrikes, 18 raptors taking large prey, and 12 raptors taking small prey.
evidence: This is stated as a fact describing the study's dataset.

claim: The final skull morphometric dataset consisted of 347 birds across 298 species.
source: Thus, the final skull morphometric dataset consisted of 347 birds across 298 species: 9 folivores, 40 frugivores, 53 generalists, 5 granivores, 175 invertivores, 26 nectarivores, 27 piscivores, 4 scavengers, and 8 tetrapod hunters.
evidence: This is stated as a fact describing the study's dataset.

claim: Presence of a rhamphotheca is known to reduce stress experienced during a bite.
source: Presence of a rhamphotheca is known to reduce stress experienced during a bite (Lautenschlager et al., 2013)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Lautenschlager et al., 2013.

claim: Skull length generally increases with body mass with a scaling exponent of 2.75 (slightly negative allometry, R2 = 0.63) for the extant birds sampled.
source: Through log10-log10 regression, we found that skull length generally increases with body mass with a scaling exponent of 2.75 (slightly negative allometry, R2 = 0.63) for the extant birds sampled.
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of skull length and body mass data.

claim: A total of 56 taxa are included in the qualitative ancestral state reconstruction.
source: A total of 56 taxa are included in the qualitative ancestral state reconstruction.
evidence: This is stated as a fact describing the study's methodology.

claim: 14 of 30 (47%) of diets in the qualitative reconstruction are supported by preserved meal evidence or quantitative diet proxies.
source: In total, 14 of 30 (47%) of diets in this reconstruction are supported by preserved meal evidence or quantitative diet proxies.
evidence: This is stated as a fact describing the study's dataset.

claim: A total of 44 taxa are used in ancestral state reconstruction of body mass.
source: A total of 44 taxa are used in ancestral state reconstruction of body mass, 13 in upper jaw MA, 9 in lower jaw MA, 13 in FEA, and 16 in pedal TM.
evidence: This is stated as a fact describing the study's methodology.

claim: Sapeornis was used as the outgroup in ancestral state reconstruction.
source: Sapeornis was used as the outgroup in ancestral state reconstruction.
evidence: This is stated as a fact describing the study's methodology.

claim: The qualitative diet of Sapeornis was classified as herbivorous based on preserved seed meals.
source: Its qualitative diet was classified as herbivorous based on preserved seed meals (O'Connor, 2019a).
evidence: This is supported by citation to O'Connor, 2019a.

claim: Ancestral states were calculated 10,000 times with random resolutions of the polytomies and averaged.
source: As polytomies are present in the enantiornithine tree used, ancestral states were calculated 10,000 times with random resolutions of the polytomies and averaged.
evidence: This is stated as a fact describing the study's methodology.

claim: BMNHC-Ph1204 is referred to cf. Sulcavis based on multiple shared synapomorphies.
source: BMNHC-Ph1204 was previously identified to Bohaiornithidae indet. (Liu et al., 2022), though we herein refine the diagnosis to cf. Sulcavis.
evidence: This is based on morphological comparison showing shared features between BMNHC-Ph1204 and Sulcavis as detailed in the Methods section.

claim: The hypothesis of Longipteryx as a specialist piscivore can no longer be rejected based on refined mass data.
source: we believe that with this refined mass data the hypothesis of Longipteryx as a specialist piscivore (O'Connor and Chiappe, 2011a; Chiappe and Meng, 2016; Zhang et al., 2001; Wang et al., 2015b; O'Connor, 2009; Martyniuk, 2012; Chatterjee, 2015; Benito and Olivé, 2022) can no longer be rejected.
evidence: This is inferred from the finding that three Longipteryx specimens are above the mass cut-off for piscivory in the refined analysis.

claim: Every bohaiornithid is less massive than any avian obligate scavenger.
source: We note that every bohaiornithid is less massive than any avian obligate scavenger
evidence: This is based on comparison of bohaiornithid mass estimates to extant scavenger masses.

claim: Very large body size is a prerequisite for obligate scavenging.
source: Coupled with past work proposing very large body size is a prerequisite for obligate scavenging (Ruxton and Houston, 2004)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Ruxton and Houston, 2004.

claim: The extent of excursion of the upper beak in life and whether it occurs during biting is unrecorded for the vast majority of taxa.
source: Unfortunately, the extent of excursion of the upper beak in, life and whether it occurs during biting, is unrecorded for the vast majority of taxa.
evidence: This is stated as a gap in current knowledge.

claim: The quadrate is disarticulated in every published bohaiornithid skull.
source: The quadrate is disarticulated in every published bohaiornithid skull, and its position is highly influential on MA measurements.
evidence: This is stated as a fact about the fossil preservation.

claim: Folivory cannot be ruled out for any bohaiornithid based on sensitivity analysis of quadrate position.
source: Our sensitivity analysis of the quadrate position (Figure 2—figure supplement 1, Supplementary file 4) indicates that folivory cannot be ruled out for any bohaiornithid.
evidence: This is based on sensitivity analysis results as shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1 and Supplementary file 4.

claim: Bohaiornithids have some of the most robust teeth within Enantiornithes.
source: Bohaiornithids, notably, have some of the most robust teeth within Enantiornithes (O'Connor and Chiappe, 2011a).
evidence: This is supported by citation to O'Connor and Chiappe, 2011a.

claim: Several groups of extant folivorous birds have specialised hindguts to process plant matter.
source: Additionally, several groups of extant folivorous birds have specialised hindguts to process plant matter.
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on emus, geese, anseriforms, and galliforms.

claim: The Jehol climate is believed to have been highly variable and affected by local volcanic activity.
source: The Jehol climate is believed to have been highly variable and affected by local volcanic activity (Xu et al., 2020)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Xu et al., 2020.

claim: Pengornis shows signs of generalist feeding with ability to raptorially take large prey.
source: Pengornis shows signs of generalist feeding with ability to raptorially take large prey.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Miller et al., 2023.

claim: The alleged rangle (raptorial gastroliths) in Bohaiornis has been reinterpreted as postmortem mineral growth.
source: Note that the alleged rangle (raptorial gastroliths) used as previous evidence of raptorial behaviour in Bohaiornis (Li et al., 2014) has been reinterpreted as postmortem mineral growth (Liu et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Liu et al., 2021.

claim: Bohaiornithids do not display adaptations for taking foods as hard as extant birds commonly considered durophages.
source: Bohaiornithids, therefore, do not display adaptations for taking foods as hard as extant birds commonly considered durophages.
evidence: This is inferred from comparison of bohaiornithid jaw MA and FEA results to those of husking granivores and parrots.

claim: Bohaiornithid tooth shape is driven by phylogeny rather than diet.
source: Given this overlap and the ecological diversity within the group we support here, we suggest the similarity in bohaiornithid tooth shape is driven by phylogeny rather than, as proposed by Zhou et al., 2021, diet.
evidence: This is inferred from the finding that bohaiornithids have diverse diets despite similar tooth shapes.

claim: The robust teeth in Bohaiornithidae may serve as general-use tools capable of processing diverse foods effectively.
source: The robust teeth in Bohaiornithidae may serve as general-use tools capable of processing diverse foods effectively rather than adaptations to a specialised diet shared across the clade.
evidence: This is speculated based on the diversity of diets identified within Bohaiornithidae.

claim: The skull architecture of Pengornithidae is considered plesiomorphic for enantiornithines.
source: In particular, Longipterygidae and Bohaiornithidae may represent opposite evolutionary trajectories from the skull architecture of Pengornithidae, which is considered plesiomorphic for enantiornithines (Wang et al., 2021b)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Wang et al., 2021b.

claim: Longipterygids were limited by their weak and gracile jaws to relatively soft and compliant food sources.
source: Longipterygids, conversely, were limited by their weak and gracile jaws to relatively soft and compliant food sources (Miller et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Miller et al., 2022.

claim: Ancestral state reconstruction predicts a concurrent increase in body mass for Bohaiornithidae and Pengornithidae near 125 Ma.
source: Indeed, ancestral state reconstruction (Figure 9—figure supplement 1) predicts a concurrent increase in body mass for Bohaiornithidae and Pengornithidae near 125 Ma.
evidence: This is based on ancestral state reconstruction as shown in Figure 9—figure supplement 1.

claim: Ancestral state reconstruction recovers the large mass of pengornithids as convergent, not present ancestrally in the clade.
source: Interestingly, though, it recovers the large mass of pengornithids as convergent, not present ancestrally in the clade.
evidence: This is based on ancestral state reconstruction driven by the smaller size of the earliest pengornithid, Eopengornis.

claim: Hummingbirds are known to have skulls that are peramorphic relative to other Strisores.
source: Hummingbirds are known to have skulls that are peramorphic relative to other Strisores (Navalón et al., 2021)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Navalón et al., 2021.

claim: Elongation of the rostrum tends to parallel elongation of the skull in extant birds.
source: In other words, elongation of the rostrum tends to parallel elongation of the skull.
evidence: This is based on analysis of skull TM data showing positive correlation between relative rostrum length and relative skull length.

claim: The rostrum in extant birds has relatively high integration with the rest of the skull.
source: This is unsurprising as the rostrum in extant birds has relatively high integration with the rest of the skull (Tables S2 and S3 in Felice and Goswami, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Felice and Goswami, 2018.

claim: Bohaiornithids do not conform to the general correlation of increasing rostrum length and skull length seen in extant birds.
source: Bohaiornithids also do not conform to the general correlation of increasing rostrum length and skull length. If anything, those with longer skulls have shorter rostra.
evidence: This is based on analysis of skull TM data for bohaiornithids as shown in Figure 8.

claim: Crown birds ancestrally have relatively larger brains than their earlier-diverging counterparts according to one hypothesis.
source: One hypothesis proposes that crown birds ancestrally have relatively larger brains than their earlier-diverging counterparts (Torres et al., 2021)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Torres et al., 2021.

claim: A recently discovered enantiornithine basicranium displays many crown-bird-like characteristics.
source: However, a subsequently discovered enantiornithine basicranium displays many crown-bird-like characteristics and has been used to argue a crown-bird-like endocranium was present in the common ancestor of Ornithothoraces (Chiappe et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Chiappe et al., 2022.

claim: Most non-raptorial perching taxa in the original pedal TM dataset are zygodactyl or semi-zygodactyl.
source: It has come to our attention (Clark et al., 2023) that in the work our pedal morphometric results were originally reported in Miller et al., 2022 only one non-raptorial perching taxon has an anisodactyl toe arrangement, as in all known enantiornithines. Most are zygodactyl (Cuculidae, Psittaciformes) or semi-zygodactyl (Musophagidae)
evidence: This is stated as a fact about the dataset composition with citation to Clark et al., 2023.

claim: Five additional representatives of non-raptorial perching taxa with anisodactyl toe arrangements were added to the pedal TM dataset.
source: In response to this, we added an additional five representatives of non-raptorial perching taxa with anisodactyl toe arrangements (Cracidae, Fregatidae, Meropidae, Phoeniculidae, Podargidae).
evidence: This is stated as a fact about the study's methodology.

claim: The new extant pedal TM data had minimal effect on ecological category boundaries and phylogenetic signal.
source: The new extant data had minimal effect on ecological category boundaries and phylogenetic signal of pedal morphometrics.
evidence: This is based on comparison of results with and without the new data.

claim: Toe arrangement is not a driving force of the trends observed in pedal morphometric data.
source: Given the minimal change caused by adding more anisodactyl birds, that the anisodactyl birds plot alongside our zygodactyl non-raptorial perchers, and that owls (Strigidae) and the osprey (Pandionidae) are semi-zygodactyl (Botelho et al., 2015) but plot far from zygodactyl non-raptorial perchers, we believe that toe arrangement is not a driving force of the trends observed in our pedal morphometric data.
evidence: This is inferred from analysis showing minimal effect of adding anisodactyl birds and the distribution of semi-zygodactyl taxa.

claim: Zhouornis CNUVB-0903 had achieved sexual maturity but not skeletal maturity according to histological data.
source: Histological data from two bones has been used to suggest that Zhouornis CNUVB-0903 had achieved sexual maturity but not skeletal maturity (Zhang et al., 2013)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Zhang et al., 2013.

claim: A recent study has shown that histological maturity can vary greatly within individual enantiornithines but upholds the diagnosis of CNUVB-0903 as an adult.
source: A recent study (Atterholt et al., 2021) has shown that histological maturity can vary greatly within individual enantiornithines but upholds the diagnosis of CNUVB-0903 as an adult.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Atterholt et al., 2021.

claim: The indeterminate bohaiornithid CUGB P1202 is considered the least mature published member of the family.
source: The indeterminate bohaiornithid CUGB P1202 is considered the least mature published member of the family (Peteya et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Peteya et al., 2017.

claim: Subadulthood begins at or before character stage 1 and full maturity occurs after completion of character stage 3 in bohaiornithids.
source: By correlating the histological maturity of Atterholt et al., 2021 with the character stage system (Table 10), we see that subadulthood begins at or before character stage 1 and full maturity occurs after completion of character stage 3.
evidence: This is inferred from correlation of histological and character stage data as shown in Table 10.

claim: Most extant animals are considered 'mature' upon reaching the subadult stage.
source: Most extant animals are considered 'mature' upon reaching the subadult stage (Hone et al., 2016)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Hone et al., 2016.
